newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House's Oxley -- more securities reforms needed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House's Oxley -- more securities reforms needed.

text.p: The 104th Congress has enacted several bills eagerly sought by the securities industry, but much more needs to be done on Capitol Hill to eliminate overregulation of markets, Rep. Michael Oxley (R-Ohio), a key member of the House finance subcommittee, said Thursday.

"There are clearly a lot of issues left on the table that we plan to address in the early session of the 105th Congress" assuming Republicans retain control of the House and Senate, said Oxley, who would take over chairmanship of the finance subpanel of the House Commerce committee.
He said "first and foremost" would be a new bill to cut back "suitability" requirements for dealers selling securities to institutional buyers.

"I intend to hold hearings and move a bill in the 105th Congress if we are fortunate enough to retain a majority and I become chairman of the subcommittee," said Oxley, during a breakfast speech to the Public Securities Associations's fixed-income legal and compliance conference.
Oxley said his panel also would take another shot at legislation to "reform the antiquated rules of the Glass-Steagall Act.

"It has been a ping-pong ball over the years, trying to reform Glass-Steagall. I don't think anybody who knows anything about these issues would say Glass-Steagall in today's world makes any sense the way it is currently structured," Oxley said. "Efforts to take a look at totally restructuring the securities and banking laws is long, long overdue," he said.

Oxley said the subcommittee also would examine additional legislation to allow Federal regulators to pre-empt state securities standards and to simplify information that securities issuers must provide in prospectuses.

"We will be responding to the California securities litigation reform ballot issue," Oxley said. "There are several ways to skin that cat. And short of getting a bill passed, our efforts will be directed toward that state and the need to follow that initiative."
Bringing technology to the capital markets would be another priority for the subcommittee, Oxley said.

"We want to facilitate electronic transfers and make self-regulatory organizations more technically friendly," Oxley said. He also said his subcommittee would conduct oversight hearings on regulation of the municipal securities market.
The Glass-Steagall Act is a Depression-era law that separates investment and commercial banking.
